newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish state workers reject pay deal, call strike.
newsitem.headline: Spanish state workers reject pay deal, call strike.

text.p: Spanish civil servants on Thursday shrugged off a government promise of future pay raises and called a 24-hour strike for December 11 in protest at a freeze on their 1997 salaries, a union spokesman said.
The unions said they had rejected a last-ditch attempt by the conservative government to avert the strike by promising to raise 1998 and 1999 salaries in compensation for the freeze.
"We have agreed to call a strike for December 11," a union spokesman said, after the unions met to discuss the government's proposal.
Spain's Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato told a conference on Wednesday that the government was going to do "everything possible" to avert a clash with workers.
But unions appeared determined to take the government to task for its tough budget plan aimed at getting Spain in shape for European Monetary Union (EMU).
"This is more of a provocation than an offer," Carlos Sanchez, a representative of the Workers' Commission (CCOO), one of Spain's two biggest unions, told state radio.
"This is not an offer that can provide a way out from the conflict...We will tell the government again that it has to modify the offer," he continued.
Unions will next hold talks with the government on December 3, the Public Administration Ministry said.

The government sparked mass protests in July when it announced it would freeze public sector salaries in 1997. Labour leaders said they would continue their fight and would call a general strike in December if the government refused to back down.

The unions, led by the CCOO and the General Workers' Union (UGT), said the freeze violated a deal with the previous Socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise in line with inflation in 1997.
They said government workers had lost 11.2 percent of their buying power since 1993, saving the government 785 billion pesetas ($6.09 billion)in the process.
Public sector pay was frozen in 1993 and increased a mere one percent in 1994, but moved up in line with inflation in 1995 and 1996.

The Popular Party government, which made an election promise to push Spain into EMU, says the 1997 freeze is an essential part of its austere draft budget aimed at bringing the deficit down to the level required to join the single currency in 1999.
It estimates the measure will slash 200 billion pesetas off the deficit, helping to reduce it to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from a forecast 4.4 percent in 1996.
